q.q: In which year did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre take place?
q.x: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred on April 13, 1919, in Amritsar, Punjab. It was a turning point in the Indian freedom struggle as it led to widespread national outrage. General Dyer ordered the troops to open fire on the unarmed crowd.

q.q: Who was the first woman President of the Indian National Congress?
q.x: Annie Besant became the first woman president of the Indian National Congress in 1917. Sarojini Naidu was the first Indian woman to hold the position in 1925.

q.q: Which specific administrative reform introduced by Sher Shah Suri served as the primary model for the land revenue system adopted by Raja Todar Mal during Akbar's reign?
q.x: Sher Shah Suri introduced the 'Rai' system, which involved the measurement of land and the classification of soil productivity. Raja Todar Mal, who served under Sher Shah before joining Akbar, refined these principles into the formal Dahsala system. This lineage of land revenue assessment remains a cornerstone of Mughal economic history.

q.q: What was the core principle of the 'Ryotwari System' introduced by Thomas Munro in the Madras Presidency?
o: Revenue was collected by local Zamindars acting as intermediaries
Revenue was assessed directly on the individual cultivator
Revenue was fixed permanently in perpetuity
Revenue was based on communal village holdings
q.x: In the Ryotwari system, the government dealt directly with the ryots (cultivators). There was no intermediary landlord class, and the revenue assessment was subject to periodic revision, distinguishing it from the Permanent Settlement of Bengal.

q.q: The Mughal Empire was founded by which ruler?
q.x: Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526 after defeating Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat. He was a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan. His victory marked the beginning of Mughal dominance in Northern India.

q.q: Which ancient university was founded by Kumargupta I?
q.x: Nalanda, located in present-day Bihar, was one of the world's first residential universities. It was established in the 5th century AD during the Gupta period under the patronage of Kumaragupta I.

q.q: Which Mauryan edict explicitly mentions the names of five Hellenistic kings, providing crucial evidence for the diplomatic relations between Ashoka and the Western world?
q.x: Major Rock Edict XIII is unique for documenting Ashoka's diplomatic missions to the kingdoms of Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus Gonatas, Magas, and Alexander of Epirus. It provides tangible historical proof of the international reach of Mauryan diplomacy.

q.q: Who is known as the 'Iron Man of India'?
q.x: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel is known as the Iron Man of India for his role in the unification of princely states. He served as the first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister of India. His efforts were crucial in creating a unified Indian state.

q.q: Which among the following literary works was composed by the poet Kalidasa during the Gupta period?
q.x: Abhijnanashakuntalam is one of the most famous plays written by the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa. He is widely regarded as the greatest poet and dramatist of the Gupta era. The other works listed were written by different authors like Chanakya, Vishakhadatta, and Shudraka.

q.q: The 'Permanent Settlement' of 1793 in Bengal was introduced by which British Governor-General?
q.x: The Permanent Settlement, also known as the Zamindari system, was introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793. It fixed the land revenue to be paid by the Zamindars to the British East India Company. This system significantly altered the land tenure structure in Bengal.

q.q: The 'Ilbert Bill' controversy during the tenure of Lord Ripon was primarily sparked by which of the following policy changes?
o: The restriction of vernacular press freedom
The proposal to allow Indian judges to try criminal cases involving Europeans
The reduction of the age limit for the Civil Service examination
The imposition of the Vernacular Press Act
q.x: The Ilbert Bill, introduced in 1883, aimed to remove racial discrimination in the judicial system by allowing Indian judges to preside over criminal trials involving European defendants. This caused a massive backlash from the European community, leading to the bill being significantly watered down.

q.q: Who was the first Governor-General of independent India?
q.x: Lord Mountbatten served as the first Governor-General of independent India from 1947 to 1948. He was followed by C. Rajagopalachari, who was the first and only Indian Governor-General. This is a common foundational question in Indian history.

q.q: The 'Kuka Movement' was a prominent anti-British uprising located primarily in which region?
q.x: The Kuka Movement, led by Ram Singh, originated in Punjab in the 1840s as a religious purification movement. It later transformed into an anti-British political movement that advocated for the boycott of British goods, institutions, and laws. The British government suppressed the movement harshly in the 1870s.

q.q: The 'Veda Samaj', which promoted social reform and monotheism, was established in which region?
q.x: Veda Samaj was established in Madras in 1864 by K. Sridharalu Naidu and Keshab Chandra Sen. It was inspired by the Brahmo Samaj of Bengal and focused on social reform, female education, and the abolition of caste distinctions. It played a crucial role in the intellectual awakening of South India.

q.q: The Battle of Plassey was fought in which year?
q.x: The Battle of Plassey took place in 1757 between the British East India Company and the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah. This victory established British political dominance in Bengal. It is considered the beginning of British rule in India.

q.q: The famous slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' was raised by whom?
q.x: Bal Gangadhar Tilak gave this famous slogan during the Indian freedom struggle. He was a prominent leader of the Extremist faction of the Indian National Congress. His work significantly boosted the morale of Indian nationalists.

q.q: Which Buddhist council resulted in the formal schism of the Sangha into the Sthaviravada and Mahasamghika schools?
q.x: The Second Buddhist Council, held at Vaishali about 100 years after the Buddha's death, addressed disputes over monastic discipline. The failure to reach a consensus led to the first major split in Buddhism between the traditionalist Sthaviravadins and the more liberal Mahasamghikas.

q.q: The 'Swaraj Party' was formed in 1923 by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru after the failure of which major political movement?
q.x: Following the abrupt withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement by Mahatma Gandhi after the Chauri Chaura incident, a rift occurred within the Congress. C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party to pursue the policy of 'entering the councils' to obstruct the colonial government from within.

q.q: Who among the following was the founder of the 'Servants of India Society' established in 1905?
q.x: Gopal Krishna Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in Pune in 1905. The objective of the society was to train national missionaries for the service of India. It promoted social and human development and worked towards national unity.

q.q: Who wrote the famous book 'Discovery of India'?
q.x: Jawaharlal Nehru wrote 'The Discovery of India' while he was imprisoned at Ahmednagar Fort between 1942 and 1945. The book provides a comprehensive overview of Indian history and philosophy.

q.q: Who founded the Maurya Empire in ancient India?
q.x: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire in 322 BCE with the help of his mentor, Chanakya. He overthrew the Nanda dynasty to establish his rule over Magadha.

q.q: The Non-Cooperation Movement was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in which year?
q.x: Mahatma Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920. The primary goal was to resist British rule through non-violent means. It was later withdrawn by Gandhi following the Chauri Chaura incident in 1922.

q.q: Which movement was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1942?
q.x: The Quit India Movement was a major civil disobedience campaign launched in August 1942. Its main objective was to demand an end to British rule in India.

q.q: Which Buddhist Council was held at Pataliputra under the patronage of Emperor Ashoka?
q.x: The Third Buddhist Council was convened in Pataliputra around 250 BCE under the patronage of Emperor Ashoka. Moggaliputta Tissa presided over this council. Its primary goal was to settle disputes within the Sangha and purify the Buddhist scriptures.

q.q: Who among the following was the last Mughal Emperor?
q.x: Bahadur Shah Zafar was the last Mughal Emperor of India. He was deposed by the British after the 1857 Revolt and exiled to Rangoon. His death effectively ended the Mughal dynasty.

q.q: The Indus Valley Civilization is primarily known for which feature?
q.x: The Indus Valley Civilization is famous for its advanced urban planning, grid-based street layouts, and sophisticated drainage systems. These features were highly developed for the Bronze Age period.

q.q: Which ancient text is known as the oldest Veda?
q.x: The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas and one of the oldest religious texts in the world. It contains a collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns.

q.q: Which Mughal emperor is credited with building the Taj Mahal?
q.x: Shah Jahan commissioned the construction of the Taj Mahal in Agra as a mausoleum for his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It is recognized as one of the Seven Wonders of the World.

q.q: Which Gupta ruler is credited with the defeat of the Huna invader Mihirakula, as documented in the Mandasor stone inscription?
q.x: While Skandagupta is famous for early battles against the Hunas, the Mandasor inscription specifically credits Yashodharman of Malwa with the decisive defeat of the Huna king Mihirakula. This victory marked a significant turning point in the resistance against Central Asian invasions.

q.q: During the Third Anglo-Mysore War, which treaty ultimately forced Tipu Sultan to surrender half of his kingdom and pay a massive war indemnity?
q.x: The Treaty of Seringapatam, signed in 1792, concluded the Third Anglo-Mysore War. Under its harsh terms, Tipu Sultan was forced to cede half of his territories to the British and their allies and pay a significant financial indemnity.

q.q: Who presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress in 1885?
q.x: Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress held in Bombay in 1885. A.O. Hume was the retired British officer who helped organize the first session. This event marked the beginning of organized political activity in India.

q.q: Which medieval ruler is credited with shifting the capital of the Delhi Sultanate from Delhi to Daulatabad?
q.x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq made the controversial decision to shift his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad in the Deccan. His intention was to better control the southern territories of his empire. However, the move proved to be a failure due to logistical difficulties and climate issues.

q.q: Who is known as the 'Frontier Gandhi' for his role in the freedom struggle?
q.x: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, an activist in the North-West Frontier Province, was known as the 'Frontier Gandhi' or 'Badshah Khan'. He founded the Khudai Khidmatgar movement and was a staunch follower of Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy of non-violence. He remained dedicated to his principles throughout his life in Pakistan.

q.q: What was the capital of the Mauryan Empire?
q.x: Pataliputra, modern-day Patna, served as the capital of the Mauryan Empire under rulers like Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka. It was a major center of power and culture in ancient India.

q.q: Which movement is associated with the 'Salt March' of 1930?
q.x: The Salt March, also known as the Dandi March, was the opening act of the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930. Mahatma Gandhi marched to the sea to protest against the British salt tax. This event gained massive international media attention.

q.q: The Quit India Movement was started in which year?
q.x: The Quit India Movement, also known as the August Kranti, was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1942. It was a demand for an orderly British withdrawal from India. The call for 'Do or Die' became the defining slogan of this movement.

q.q: In which year did the Battle of Plassey take place?
q.x: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757 between the British East India Company and the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah. This victory solidified British influence in the Bengal region.

q.q: Who was the first Indian leader to serve as the President of the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) upon its founding in 1920?
q.x: Lala Lajpat Rai was elected the first President of the AITUC at its inaugural session in Bombay in 1920. The organization was established to provide a unified platform for the growing labor movement in India during the colonial era.

q.q: The 'Indian National Congress' was founded in which year?
q.x: The Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 in Bombay. Allan Octavian Hume played a significant role in its establishment.

q.q: Which act of the British Parliament introduced the system of 'Diarchy' in the provinces of India?
q.x: The Government of India Act 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, introduced Diarchy in the provincial governments. This system divided provincial subjects into 'reserved' and 'transferred' lists. It was an early attempt to provide limited provincial autonomy.

q.q: Which Chalukyan ruler successfully defeated Harshavardhana on the banks of the Narmada River, preventing the northward expansion of his empire?
q.x: Pulakeshin II, the most famous ruler of the Badami Chalukyas, defeated the powerful North Indian king Harshavardhana around 618-620 AD. This victory is documented in the Aihole inscription and established the Narmada River as the boundary between their respective empires.

q.q: The title 'Netaji' was bestowed upon which Indian freedom fighter?
q.x: Subhash Chandra Bose is widely known as Netaji. He led the Indian National Army (INA) and played a pivotal role in the struggle for Indian independence.

q.q: Which Governor-General of India was responsible for the 'Policy of Masterly Inactivity' regarding the North-West Frontier of British India?
q.x: Sir John Lawrence, who served as Viceroy from 1864 to 1869, championed the 'Policy of Masterly Inactivity.' This involved avoiding interference in the internal affairs of Afghanistan to prevent overextension and maintain stability along the turbulent North-West Frontier.

q.q: The 'Treaty of Purandar' (1665) was signed between the Mughal Empire and which Maratha leader?
q.x: The Treaty of Purandar was signed between Shivaji Maharaj and Jai Singh I, representing the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb. As per the treaty, Shivaji had to surrender a significant number of forts to the Mughals and agree to serve the empire. This was a tactical retreat for the Marathas during a period of intense pressure.

q.q: Who founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828?
q.x: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj to reform Hindu society and promote monotheism. He is often referred to as the 'Father of Modern India' for his social reform efforts.

q.q: What was the main purpose of the 'Cripps Mission' that visited India in 1942?
o: To secure Indian cooperation for the war effort
q.x: The Cripps Mission was sent by the British government to India during World War II to gain support from the Indian National Congress for the war effort. In return, the mission promised self-government and the framing of a new constitution after the war. The Congress eventually rejected the proposal due to its lack of a firm timeline for independence.

q.q: Who was the author of the epic 'Ramayana'?
q.x: The ancient Sanskrit epic Ramayana is traditionally attributed to the sage Valmiki. It is one of the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India, the other being the Mahabharata.

q.q: Which empire was known as the 'Golden Age of India'?
q.x: The Gupta Empire is widely regarded as the Golden Age of India due to significant advancements in science, literature, and art. This period saw the development of many fundamental mathematical concepts.

q.q: In the context of the socio-religious reform movements in 19th-century India, what was the primary objective of the 'Dharma Sabha' founded by Radha Kanta Deb?
o: To support the abolition of Sati
To oppose the Brahmo Samaj's reformist agenda
To advocate for the political independence of Bengal
q.x: The Dharma Sabha was formed in 1830 by Radha Kanta Deb as an orthodox response to the reformist activities of Raja Ram Mohan Roy. Its primary goal was to protect traditional Hindu practices and oppose the influence of the Brahmo Samaj, particularly regarding the prohibition of Sati.

q.q: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred in which city?
q.x: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on April 13, 1919, in Amritsar, Punjab. It was a tragic event where British troops opened fire on a peaceful crowd.

q.q: Which famous slogan was given by Subhash Chandra Bose?
q.x: Subhash Chandra Bose popularized the slogan 'Jai Hind' to inspire the Indian National Army. While Bal Gangadhar Tilak said 'Swaraj is my birthright', Mahatma Gandhi coined 'Do or Die'.

q.q: Who was the founder of the Maurya Empire?
q.x: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire in ancient India with the help of his mentor Chanakya. He overthrew the Nanda dynasty to establish his rule. His empire eventually spanned most of the Indian subcontinent.

q.q: Who is famously known as the 'Iron Man of India'?
q.x: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel earned the title 'Iron Man of India' for his role in integrating the various princely states into a unified Indian nation after independence.

q.q: The famous 'Battle of Wandiwash' in 1760 was fought between the British and which other European power?
q.x: The Battle of Wandiwash was a decisive conflict in the Third Carnatic War. The British forces defeated the French army, effectively ending French imperial ambitions in India. This victory consolidated British supremacy in the Indian subcontinent.
